name: Afsharid Empire

fields.foundation: The Afsharid Empire was founded in 1736 by Nader Shah, a military commander who had risen from a modest background in the Turkic Afshar tribe of Khorasan to become the most powerful man in Iran before formally seizing the throne. Before proclaiming himself Shah, Nader was known as Tahmasp Qoli Khan and served as the leading general of the Safavid claimant Tahmasp II. In that office he had already driven out all three foreign occupiers of Iranian territory. He defeated the Ghilzai Afghans at Damghan and Murche-Khort and expelled them from Isfahan in 1729, freeing the Safavid capital after seven years of occupation. He pushed the Ottomans back in a series of western campaigns. He also induced Russia to return its Caspian conquests through the Treaties of Resht (1732) and Ganja (1735). By March 1736, when Nader set aside the infant Safavid Abbas III and was proclaimed Shah after a great assembly on the Mughan plain, he commanded a large, battle-hardened army and had restored Iran's western and northern frontiers. The proclamation of the Afsharid dynasty therefore made formal a military supremacy he already held: years of warfare had restored Iranian territory and political unity before he took the crown. His legitimacy rested almost entirely on military success, and not on dynastic genealogy or religious sanction. That gave the empire its power, and it was also why the empire collapsed so quickly upon his death.
fields.socioeconomy: The Afsharid economy was caught between very heavy military spending and the lack of a revenue system that could sustain it. Nader Shah's incessant campaigns imposed crushing taxation on the Iranian population, and contemporary observers described provinces so exhausted that they could barely support his armies. The Indian campaign of 1738–1739 brought temporary relief on a spectacular scale. The sack of Delhi and the seizure of the Mughal imperial treasury yielded wealth that contemporaries estimated at hundreds of millions of rupees, so much that Nader remitted taxes throughout Iran for three years. The Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor and Darya-i-Noor diamonds were among the prizes carried back to Persia, together with large numbers of artisans and craftsmen. The windfall hid the fiscal weakness of the Afsharid state without curing it. The empire had no developed commerce apart from what its armies extracted. Trade routes that had functioned under Safavid patronage were disrupted by constant warfare, urban populations were impoverished by exceptional tax demands, and the agricultural base of central and western Iran was damaged by the decades of conflict that preceded and followed Nader's accession. The Persian Gulf trade through Bushehr and Bandar Abbas continued, and Nader's intervention in Oman, which ended in the capture of Muscat around 1743, extended Iranian reach into the Arabian Sea. These revenues were not enough to sustain an empire held together by military force.
fields.military: Nader Shah's military record is among the most notable in the history of warfare, and historians have often compared him with Alexander the Great, Genghis Khan and Timur. His army combined Persian, Turkic, Afghan, Kurdish and Georgian contingents under a unified command, and it was exceptionally disciplined and flexible in its tactics. He fought every kind of war: set-piece battles, above all Karnal (February 1739), where he crushed a Mughal army several times larger in a few hours; sieges; mountain warfare; naval operations in the Persian Gulf; and strategic campaigning across great distances. The Indian campaign was perhaps his most spectacular achievement. Forcing the Khyber Pass in late 1738, he took Peshawar, crossed the Indus, occupied Lahore and, after Karnal, entered Delhi in March 1739. In 1740 he campaigned in Central Asia, subduing Bukhara and Khiva, while keeping up military pressure on the Ottomans in the west, which ended in his victory at Kars in 1745. Nader made systematic use of musket-armed troops, the jazayerchis or jezzailchis, and of mobile field artillery, including swivel guns carried by camels (zamburaks), and he combined their firepower with his strong cavalry. His naval programme, which built a Persian Gulf fleet largely from scratch, showed ambitions that went beyond land warfare. The army was nonetheless intensely personal: there was no professional officer corps or institutional training system independent of Nader himself.
fields.governance: The Afsharid Empire had almost no means of government independent of Nader Shah's personal authority. The Safavid dynasty he replaced had built a developed administrative apparatus over more than two centuries. Nader, by contrast, governed through personal military command, officials answerable directly to him, and taxation so intensive that it verged on the systematic spoliation of his own territories. There was no stable vizierate, no codified administrative law and little bureaucratic continuity between the Safavid structures he inherited and the Afsharid state he created. Provincial government was typically assigned to military commanders, often kinsmen, fellow Afshars or trusted lieutenants from his campaigns, whose chief task was to extract revenue and not to administer. Nader attempted one significant institutional innovation. At the Mughan assembly in 1736 he proposed that Twelver Shi'ism be recognised as a fifth school of Sunni jurisprudence, the Ja'fari madhhab. This would have placed Iran between Sunni and Shi'a Islam and eased the integration of his Sunni Afghan and Central Asian subjects. Although he pursued the idea through diplomacy and the religious conference at Najaf in 1743, the Ottomans never accepted it, the Shi'a clergy resented it, and it lapsed with his death. In his later years Nader grew more suspicious and cruel, and in 1742 he had his eldest son Reza Qoli blinded on suspicion of plotting an assassination attempt. This hastened the decay of whatever administrative coherence the empire possessed.
fields.impact: The Afsharid Empire was a great power for only eleven years, but it changed the political geography of the Middle East and South Asia far more than so brief a span would suggest. Nader Shah's sack of Delhi in 1739 dealt a psychological and material blow to the Mughal Empire from which it never recovered. The loss of the imperial treasury undermined the finances of Mughal authority, hastened the empire's break-up into competing successor states, and helped create the power vacuum that the British East India Company and other European companies would eventually fill. The Peacock Throne, carried off to Persia and lost after Nader's death, became a symbol of the impoverishment of Mughal sovereignty. His Central Asian campaigns temporarily reasserted Iranian influence over Bukhara, Khiva and the lands beyond the Oxus, regions that had long been outside Iranian political control. His Persian Gulf fleet and intervention in Oman showed naval ambitions that later Iranian dynasties proved unable to sustain. The empire's collapse after 1747 made possible an independent Afghan state. Ahmad Shah Durrani, formerly commander of Nader's Abdali Afghan contingent, was chosen as ruler at Kandahar within months of Nader's death and founded the Durrani Empire that became the basis of modern Afghanistan. In Iran itself, the Afsharid interlude was followed by half a century of division under the Zands and rival claimants before the Qajars reunified the country.
fields.decline: The Afsharid Empire did not decline gradually. It collapsed abruptly, and few empires show so plainly what it means to depend on a single ruler. Nader Shah was assassinated by his own officers on the night of 19–20 June 1747 at Fathabad near Quchan, after a plot involving commanders of his guard, including his own kinsmen, who had become convinced that his increasingly erratic and brutal behaviour threatened their lives. Disintegration began at once. Ahmad Khan Abdali, who had led Nader's Afghan contingent, withdrew to Kandahar and was proclaimed Ahmad Shah later that year, founding the Durrani Empire and taking Afghanistan and the eastern territories with him. In Georgia, Teimuraz II and his son Erekle II consolidated effective independence in Kartli and Kakheti, and the khanates of the South Caucasus and Dagestan threw off Persian control. In western Iran, rival chieftains fought for power until Karim Khan Zand emerged as master of most of the Iranian heartland. Within a few years the empire that had stretched from the Caucasus to the Indus had contracted to a contested rump in Khorasan. The civil war between Nader's nephew Adil Shah and his brother Ibrahim Shah (1747–1748) reduced even this remnant to chaos. Shahrokh Shah, Nader's grandson, blinded in 1750, survived as a nominal ruler in Mashhad until 1796, when Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar took the city and had Shahrokh tortured to reveal the remaining Afsharid treasures. He died of his injuries, and the dynasty effectively came to an end. The Afsharid state rose from obscurity to become one of the most powerful of its age within a decade and broke apart from that peak almost overnight, a course with few parallels in history.
fields.summary: The Afsharid Empire is history's most extreme example of the one-man state. It rose from nothing to the first rank of world powers in little more than a decade and fragmented almost immediately after its founder's death. It left few institutions, no effective successor and little continuity, only the legend of Nader Shah.
fields.teaser: Nader Shah, sometimes called the Napoleon of Persia, briefly reunited Iran and campaigned from Delhi to the Caucasus. His sack of Delhi in 1739 dealt the Mughal Empire a blow from which it never recovered.
fields.t0: Nader Shah, a general from the Afshar tribe, expelled Iran's occupiers and crowned himself Shah in 1736.
fields.t1: His 1739 sack of Delhi crippled the Mughal Empire and brought the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor to Persia.
fields.t2: Built on one man's military genius, the empire shattered within months of his assassination in 1747.
fields.dyk: The treasure Nader Shah took from Delhi in 1739 was so large that he remitted taxes throughout Iran for three years.
